 Jehovahs Witnesses Relax Blood Rules After Texas Man Dies
 Michael Carter

 14

 Share 
 WhatsApp 
 Isaac Valdez suffered an epileptic seizure, and his condition deteriorated rapidly. 
 Smallest Font 
 Largest Font 
 A change to the blood transfusion policy of Jehovah's Witnesses came just 23 days after a 26-year-old Texas man died because his religious beliefs prevented him from receiving potentially life-saving treatment. Isaac Valdez suffered a brain haemorrhage after an epileptic seizure in August 2026, but his refusal of blood transfusions complicated emergency medical care.
 Valdez was browsing at a local library when he experienced the seizure, convulsed and struck his head against the ground. He subsequently lost consciousness and was taken to a hospital, where doctors discovered bleeding in his brain.
 Advertisement 
 Scroll To Continue with Content 
 His religious restrictions prevented doctors from performing a procedure to drain fluid from his brain because it could involve a blood transfusion. His family, who live in Waxahachie, Texas, initially saw signs of improvement when he regained consciousness and began speaking again.
 Also Read

 However, his condition deteriorated, and he eventually fell into a coma. A neurosurgeon informed the family that emergency surgery requiring a blood transfusion was the only way to save his life.
 The family decided to respect his lifelong religious position. Doctors withdrew his life support, and Isaac died on 26 August 2026.
 Isaac's twin brother, Jacob Valdez, described him as an intelligent person who enjoyed volunteering and helping elderly people. Jacob questioned the religious leadership's timing after the policy changed less than a month after his brother's death.
 Also Read 
 Jenny McCarthy Moves Into Outdoor Tent After Mold Illness 
 The updated policy, announced by the Governing Body of Jehovah's Witnesses, allows followers to make individual decisions about accepting most medical procedures involving donated blood components. The change effectively removes restrictions on many treatments that were previously prohibited.
 Jacob had already left the religious organization in which he was raised. Following Isaac's death, he contacted prominent members of his brother's congregation in Texas to express his frustration.
 In his messages, Jacob challenged the congregation to consider
 Also Read

 "the part you played in encouraging so many people to sacrifice their life for something that was never God's will"
 and questioned the consequences of the previous policy.
 Most recipients did not respond. One congregation elder replied that he did not understand Jacob's anger or his continued focus on the policy change.
 Also Read 
 Family Funding Helps Bring Sanfilippo Gene Therapy to Patients 
 Jacob said he wanted the organization's decision-makers to acknowledge the consequences of their previous position and take responsibility for the deaths associated with it.
 "I want to ask them if they could apologise directly, I would like not to have a deflected answer, just straightforward apology," Jacob said.
 The original prohibition dates back to 1945, when Jehovah's Witnesses leaders ruled that followers could not accept blood transfusions. The decision was based on their interpretation of biblical passages in both the Old and New Testaments that instruct believers to abstain from consuming blood.
 Also Read 
 Iowa Cancer Concerns Renew Calls to Fund Water Protection Program 
 One passage comes from the Book of Acts, which instructs Christians to abstain from blood, food offered to idols and things that have been strangled.
 Paul Gillies, an international spokesperson for Jehovah's Witnesses, described the latest decision as an updated application of biblical principles in light of modern medicine.
 "The change is basically the application of Bible principles to modern medicine and its methods," Gillies said.
 Also Read 
 Obamacare Premiums Set to Rise 13 Percent in 2027 
 Speaking at the organization's UK headquarters in Essex, Gillies maintained that the fundamental religious teaching remains unchanged. He said the prohibition on transfusing whole blood continues to apply.
 However, modern medical procedures frequently use individual blood components rather than whole blood. The revised policy permits followers to decide whether to accept components such as plasma, red blood cells and platelets.
 Gillies explained that the biblical instruction concerns
 "abstaining from blood"
 rather than
 "various components that could be extracted from blood"
 . He said the Governing Body wanted to avoid scriptural
 "overreach"
 by limiting restrictions to what the Bible explicitly describes.
 The explanation has raised questions about why the original prohibition was introduced in 1945 and why the revision took decades, particularly as medical procedures using individual blood components had already become common.
 Gillies acknowledged the concerns of families affected by the previous policy and expressed sympathy for those who have lost relatives.
 "We're sympathetic to their feelings, and if individuals have lost family members and are concerned about some of these questions, they deserve to be heard compassionately," Gillies said.
 Research published in the medical journal Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey in 2016 estimated that approximately 1,100 Jehovah's Witnesses died annually after refusing medical treatment involving blood transfusions. The exact worldwide annual death toll remains difficult to establish among the religion's estimated nine million followers.
